title: Oral history listening room
brief:
Complete the following real project in the current, initially empty directory. Choose the deliverables, media, tools, structure and implementation that serve the intended user. Build usable artifacts and check your work. Deliver the project itself. Omit personally identifying credits, author signatures and model or toolchain identity labels. No network access or credentials are provided.

Design the visitor experience for a local history room presenting six fictional audio interviews about a former indoor market. The topics are early deliveries, stall displays, lunch breaks, price signs, closing routines, and the annual winter fair. The room has two seated listening stations, a single entrance, and space for one wall panel. Typical visits last eight minutes. Create coordinated materials that let visitors choose a topic, locate it at either station, and share the space when both seats are occupied. Use the topic descriptions as content inputs and build the presentation with free offline tools. Start from an empty directory and choose the deliverables and file layout.

files.name: README.md
files.body:
# Under One Roof

An eight-minute drop-in listening room about a fictional former indoor market. Each ticket opens a short conversation with a market worker. Both seats offer the same six tickets.

## Set up the room

- Print **print/Wall panel.pdf** as one A2 portrait sheet at actual size. Mount it where visitors coming through the entrance can see it and step aside to read. Leave a waiting spot beside the panel, outside the door swing and the path to both seats.
- Print **print/Reading sheet.pdf** double-sided on A4, flipping on the long edge. Put several loose copies in a holder beside the panel. Visitors can read all six interviews here, including anyone who prefers to skip the headphones.
- Place a screen and headphones at each seat, within sight of the waiting spot. Copy this whole project folder onto each station computer. Open **index.html** locally in a browser and use full screen. Keep the audio folder, scripts, illustration and stylesheet beside the page in their supplied locations.
- Try a ticket at each seat, press the audio play control and adjust the headphones to a comfortable starting volume. Select **All topics / finish turn** to stop playback and restore the chooser.

## A visit

Allow roughly one minute to browse the panel. Visitors can begin with any number, find the same ticket on either screen, and listen, pause, replay or read. Each recording lasts 30–34 seconds. With a seat free and nobody waiting, there is time to explore several in an eight-minute visit.

When both seats are in use, arriving visitors browse the reading copies beside the panel. When a seat opens, the person who arrived first takes it. Each seated listener finishes one interview and offers the seat if someone is waiting. Visitors who want another turn can rejoin the wait. The entrance also serves as the exit.

files.name: interviews.js
files.body:
const interviews = [
  {
    "id": "01",
    "title": "Early deliveries",
    "role": "The porter",
    "tease": "A chalk line for the first cart.",
    "lines": [
      "Where did the first cart stop?",
      "Right on the chalk line by the side door. If the wheels went over it, the baker couldn't swing his trays round. My first job was to draw that line. In winter I'd be doing it by the light off the bicycle lamp.",
      "What came in first?",
      "Usually pears. You could stack potatoes any way up, but pears wore every thumbprint. We'd pass the boxes along, one pair of hands to the next. By the time the front doors opened, I'd handled half the market and hadn't bought a thing."
    ],
    "duration": 33
  },
  {
    "id": "02",
    "title": "Stall displays",
    "role": "The fruit seller",
    "tease": "Why one apple sat apart.",
    "lines": [
      "Which part of the stall did you dress first?",
      "The front lip. I'd fold a sack along it, tuck the ends under, then set the apples in the fold. Everyone thought they stayed up by themselves. A child once pulled the sack to see. We were still fishing apples out from under the fish counter at dinner.",
      "Did you change the display after that?",
      "I left one apple out on its own. That was the one you could pick up, smell, turn over. People wanted to touch something before they bought it. So did I."
    ],
    "duration": 31
  },
  {
    "id": "03",
    "title": "Lunch breaks",
    "role": "The tea counter cook",
    "tease": "A chipped cup kept a place.",
    "lines": [
      "How did anybody get away for lunch?",
      "You turned your cup upside down on my counter. That told me you were waiting for someone to mind your stall. Once you got free, you turned it right side up and I poured. One man had the same chipped cup for twenty years.",
      "Did you ever get a turn yourself?",
      "The flower girls took the kettle at half past one. Dreadful tea, the pair of them. But they'd warm my plate on the lid, and there'd be a chair pulled out where the sun fell through the high window."
    ],
    "duration": 31
  },
  {
    "id": "04",
    "title": "Price signs",
    "role": "The ticket writer",
    "tease": "The price of a crooked seven.",
    "lines": [
      "What did you write the prices on?",
      "Little black boards with a tin foot. I'd rest one on my knee and cut a point on the chalk. A broad stroke for the price, a thin one for the weight. Once my seven looked so much like a one that a whole queue formed for the butter.",
      "What did the butter seller do?",
      "Sold the first pat for one penny. Then she gave me a wet rag and stood beside me till I'd crossed the seven. Every seven I wrote after that had a bar you could see from the door."
    ],
    "duration": 30
  },
  {
    "id": "05",
    "title": "Closing routines",
    "role": "The caretaker",
    "tease": "A loose coin on the shutters.",
    "lines": [
      "How could you tell when everyone had gone?",
      "You couldn't tell by looking. Someone was always bent down behind a counter. I'd run a penny along the shutters as I walked. If somebody was still packing they'd knock twice from the other side, and I'd leave their lamp on.",
      "What was the last thing you did?",
      "Lifted the mat at the front door. Buttons, hairpins, sometimes a key. I'd put the lot in a saucer on the sill. First thing next morning there'd be somebody there, patting their coat and looking hopeful."
    ],
    "duration": 31
  },
  {
    "id": "06",
    "title": "Annual winter fair",
    "role": "The ribbon seller",
    "tease": "A ribbon measured in armfuls.",
    "lines": [
      "What changed for the winter fair?",
      "All year the stalls kept to their own squares. For the fair we ran one red ribbon the length of the aisle. The butcher held one end and I walked backwards with the reel. Every stall tied something to it. A paper bird, a bell, a wooden spoon.",
      "How did you know how much ribbon to bring?",
      "One year I measured the aisle in armfuls. Forgot to leave anything for the knots. The last stretch was a bootlace from the cobbler. After that, even when we had enough, we always finished with a bootlace."
    ],
    "duration": 34
  }
];

files.body:
# Under One Roof

A local history room about a former indoor market. Six fictional interviewees describe the work, favors and small mishaps that shaped a day in the hall, plus the annual winter fair.

## Set up the room

1. Print [the wall panel](print/wall-panel-A2.pdf) in color at A2 portrait (420 × 594 mm). Mount it on the inside wall beside the entrance so visitors can read it off to one side, with the doorway and route to both seats clear.
2. Print [the station labels](print/station-labels-letter.pdf) on one US Letter sheet and cut around the two cards. Put A at one seat and B at the other, where both letters can be seen from the panel. The letters identify seats. Each seat has the same six interviews in the same order.
3. Copy the entire [station folder](station/) to each station. Open [station/index.html](station/index.html) in a modern browser directly from the local files. Keep the folder intact so the recordings load. Connect headphones at each seat, set a comfortable volume, and leave the browser open to **Choose an interview**. The station runs offline and works with touch, mouse or keyboard.

## How a visit works

Visitors pick a topic at the wall and match its two-digit number at the next free seat. They can play the audio or open **Read transcript**. If both seats are occupied, visitors choose while they wait to one side and take whichever seat opens first. When someone is waiting, visitors give up the seat after one interview. **All interviews** stops playback and returns the screen to the topic list.

The recordings run 45–53 seconds each, about 4 minutes 53 seconds in total. Within a typical eight-minute visit there is time to orient, wait through a short turn, and listen. When seats are free, visitors can hear several interviews.

Before opening the room, try the same topic at both seats with the devices offline. Check that each headphone set plays at a comfortable level, the on-screen transcript opens, and a visitor can read the panel without blocking the doorway.

files.name: station/interviews.js
files.body:
const interviews = [
  {
    "number": "01",
    "slug": "early-deliveries",
    "title": "Early deliveries",
    "role": "Produce porter",
    "teaser": "Crates through the side door before dawn.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "How did you know the first delivery had arrived?"
      ],
      [
        "Produce porter",
        "You heard the trolley wheels strike the iron strip at the side door. Two knocks, very close together. It was still dark in the hall. The baker had one light on, and we steered by that until someone reached the switches. The cabbage crates were easy. You could stack them high. The pears had to stay on top because the man who packed them always tucked the small ripe ones along the edge."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What happened once everything was inside?"
      ],
      [
        "Produce porter",
        "We chalked the stall numbers on the crate ends. I used to put a stroke through my sevens after I left a whole load of onions at stall one. Then we'd haul the empties back to the door. When I heard the front shutters go up, I knew the floor had to be clear. Customers saw the first neat row of pears. We saw the damp rectangles where the crates had been."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 53
  },
  {
    "number": "02",
    "slug": "stall-displays",
    "title": "Stall displays",
    "role": "Fruit seller",
    "teaser": "How a fruit seller built a display that held.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What went out first on your stall?"
      ],
      [
        "Fruit seller",
        "The empty boxes. We turned them over, put the tallest ones at the back, and covered the lot with green cloth. From the aisle it looked like one great bank of apples. Behind it there was just room for my tea and a pair of scissors. I put the yellow apples next to the red ones so you could see where one sort ended and the next began."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "Did people pick straight from the display?"
      ],
      [
        "Fruit seller",
        "They could. That was the test of whether I'd built it properly. One morning a boy took an apple from the bottom and the whole corner came down. His mother was trying to catch them in her shopping bag. After that I kept the bottom row in shallow trays. And I put the tasting slices down at the front, where he could reach them next time."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 48
  },
  {
    "number": "03",
    "slug": "lunch-breaks",
    "title": "Lunch breaks",
    "role": "Sewing stall assistant",
    "teaser": "A shared kettle and a favor between neighbors.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "Where did you go for lunch?"
      ],
      [
        "Sewing stall assistant",
        "Usually just behind the stall. There was a folding chair between the spare reels and a stack of cardboard boxes. The woman next door sold buttons, and we took turns boiling the kettle by the washbasin. You brought your own mug because the spare ones somehow always walked off. I had a blue enamel one with a chip exactly where I liked to drink."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "Who watched the stall while you ate?"
      ],
      [
        "Sewing stall assistant",
        "If someone wanted a spool of black thread, my neighbor could find it. If they came with a coat and wanted a zip the exact length, she'd lean round the curtain and call me. So you learned to eat a sandwich in halves. I'd wrap the second half up again, serve the customer, then sit down. Some days I opened that same sandwich four times."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 48
  },
  {
    "number": "04",
    "slug": "price-signs",
    "title": "Price signs",
    "role": "Sign writer",
    "teaser": "Brush, card and prices you could read from the aisle.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What made a good price sign?"
      ],
      [
        "Sign writer",
        "The figures had to be big enough to read from the next stall. I used a flat brush and cut the cards out of old packing boxes. If you left the price until last, you'd run out of space, so I painted the figures first. Then came the name and the bit that said whether that bought you a pound or a whole bag."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What if the price changed halfway through the day?"
      ],
      [
        "Sign writer",
        "I'd keep a few blank cards under the counter. One Saturday the last of the plums were getting soft, and the stallholder wanted them down to half price. I made a fresh sign, but the old one was still stuck on the back of the crate, facing the other aisle. Two customers met in the middle and compared prices. They both got the cheaper bag."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 48
  },
  {
    "number": "05",
    "slug": "closing-routines",
    "title": "Closing routines",
    "role": "Hall caretaker",
    "teaser": "The sweep, the shutters and one last walk.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "How did you start closing the hall?"
      ],
      [
        "Hall caretaker",
        "I walked from the back to the front with the broom over my shoulder. That was enough. People knew they had time to sell one more thing before I came back with the dustpan. Under the stalls you'd find paper bands from the greens, the odd dropped coin, and those little wire ties that caught in the broom. I'd leave any coins on the stall ledge."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What did you check before you locked up?"
      ],
      [
        "Hall caretaker",
        "Taps first, then the doors. I pulled each latch by hand because one could look shut and still bounce open. The fish seller was usually last out. He'd put his apron in a bucket and carry it home on the bus. With the shutters down, you could hear the clock above the entrance. During the day I used to wonder whether it was even ticking."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 45
  },
  {
    "number": "06",
    "slug": "winter-fair",
    "title": "Winter fair",
    "role": "Fair volunteer",
    "teaser": "Paper stars and a different kind of market day.",
    "turns": [
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "What changed when the winter fair came around?"
      ],
      [
        "Fair volunteer",
        "Once a year we cleared the middle aisle for the fair. The regular stalls stayed open, but we put a long table down the center for the raffle. The children cut stars from paper and I climbed the steps to string them above the table. We used cotton thread. You couldn't see it from below, so the stars seemed to hang there by themselves."
      ],
      [
        "Interviewer",
        "Is there one fair you remember best?"
      ],
      [
        "Fair volunteer",
        "The year the raffle tickets went damp. A pan of hot cider was steaming right beside the tin, and the tickets came out in clumps. We spread them on the bread stall to dry and drew the numbers a little late. Nobody minded. People stayed to see who'd get the knitted blanket. The man who won it put it round his shoulders and finished his shopping."
      ]
    ],
    "seconds": 51
  }
];
